extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students in linguistics, semantics, and humor studies (scholars analysing jokes/stand-up performance)
extracted.subtask_description: A bottom-up formal method for analysing jokes: assign comedic categories, build real and imaginary ontologies, identify performatives, and analyse the utterer’s intentions via Grice’s Cooperative Principle. The procedure converts object-language descriptions into a meta-language (using a denotation function) to show who/what does what and why the joke is funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign comedic categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign one or more comedic categories to a given joke (e.g., character, reference, shock, parody, hyperbole, wordplay, madcap, analogy, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use categories as an early indicator of what elements will be important in the joke and to guide subsequent analysis (ontology and performatives). Prefer overarching categories rather than exhaustively listing every micro-element, but be aware of ambiguity and overlap (some jokes may plausibly belong to additional categories). Example anti-pattern: omitting relevant categories (e.g., failing to note wordplay in a song/rap).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify real and imaginary ontologies (ORe and OIm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct the state-of-affairs for the joke and split it into a real ontology (ORe) describing the on-stage situation and an imaginary ontology (OIm) describing events/characters narrated or retold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify sets of entities (E_Re, E_Im) and actions (I_Re, I_Im). Imaginary ontologies arise when the performer retells past events or uses fictional characters; real ontologies describe present performative elements. Use lines/segments of the text/performance to justify inclusion. Example: S4 had E_Re = {BO, BOOK, STOOL, MICROPHONE, SPEAKERS, AUDIENCE} and E_Im = {ANDY, MILLIE, BILLY, FROG, TURTLE, CROCODILE}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use denotation assignment (Fda) to map object-language to meta-language
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert elements of the object-language ontologies into meta-language entities (N Re, P Re, N Im, P Im) using a denotation assignment function (Fda) so predicates show which entities perform which actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit two-place/three-place predicate assignments (e.g., fall = {(bottle, stool)} means 'the bottle falls off the stool'). This step resolves who is doing what; anti-pattern: leaving ontology sets without linking entities to actions (OS lists only E and I but not which element performs which action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and categorise performatives (Austin’s framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the performative acts invoked in the joke (e.g., storytelling, lying, insulting, misleading) and determine the felicity conditions/requirements for these performatives to be successfully performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse which requirements are met or violated (e.g., storytelling often carries expectations like a moral or satisfying ending). Use performative requirements to locate deliberate deviations that contribute to humour (e.g., Bo 'lies' to the audience, or abuses storytelling tropes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse utterer’s intentions with Grice’s Cooperative Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse the performer’s intentions and meaning in light of Gricean maxims and the Cooperative Principle; identify when the utterer opts out, modifies, or obeys the principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine how opting out or modifying the Cooperative Principle creates audience expectations and how violating those expectations produces humour. Evidence of misleading (e.g., audience laughter/applause) supports claims that the audience was misled. Note modified cooperative behaviour (a performer may adopt their own internal 'set of rules').

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow a bottom-up, linear procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a staged order for analysis: (1) formal semantics/ontology, (2) Austin’s performatives, (3) Gricean intention/meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This linearity provides clear progression answering who (ontology), how (performatives), and why (intention/meaning). Use this order to structure the analysis and to ensure each step feeds into the next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comedic categories to inform ontology and performative selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the assigned comedic categories guide what elements to include in ontologies and which performatives to consider (e.g., a character-focused joke should prompt attention to character performatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categories narrow the analytic focus (e.g., if 'character' is prominent, focus on what characters do). However, be cautious: categories are interpretive and may be applied liberally or conservatively; justify category choices with textual/performance evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use audience reactions as evidence for felicity of performatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Take audience responses (laughter, clapping, cheering) as empirical support that a performative (e.g., misleading) achieved its intended effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such reactions as probabilistic evidence that the audience accepted the intended misdirection or deception; discuss limits of this inference and alternative explanations where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly state grammatical/conversion rules when formalising semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: When converting object-language grammatical/syntactic forms into the meta-language, explicitly state the conversion rules (e.g., GR1obj → GR1meta) to preserve formal rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to state these rules is a methodological weakness: the denotation assignment must be grounded in stated grammatical mappings. Anti-pattern: omitting GR1obj/GR1meta rules and relying on informal liberties, which undermines a strict formal semantics claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link ontological description to performative felicity conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the identified entities/actions in the ontologies to determine whether the felicity conditions of relevant performatives are met or violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: storytelling performative requires a teller, audience, narrative structure and often a moral; identify which of these are present or absent and discuss how absence (e.g., no moral, bad ending) contributes to humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect genre/trope expectations (rule-of-three, happy ending, MacGuffin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify standard narrative or genre tropes (e.g., rule-of-three, protagonist overcoming trials, acquiring MacGuffin, happy ending) and evaluate how the joke conforms to or subverts them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse whether deviations (e.g., protagonist eaten instead of triumphing) are used deliberately for comic effect. Use specific textual lines to support claims about trope invocation and subversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about scope and limits when assigning categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that category assignments are interpretive and that different choices (overarching vs exhaustive lists) change analytic focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss trade-offs: choosing fewer, overarching categories simplifies analysis but may miss subtle devices; listing all possible categories is comprehensive but may dilute the central analytic thread. Provide justification for the strategy adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ontology + performatives to trace how actions produce comic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine the ontology (who/what/does) with performative analysis to explain mechanistically how a joke produces humour (e.g., misdirection via performative lying, physical madcap routines that instantiate a pun).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show via predicates and performative requirements how a performer's actions (e.g., lifting a stool to mime 'stools') instantiate the intended comedic reading and punchline linkage.
